item.title: Jatoba DBMS now uses AI to automatically detect personal data
item.description:
We have introduced a new feature for our cyber-secure domestic general-purpose DBMS "Yatoba". The system has replaced manual labor in searching for personal data with artificial intelligence scanning. Thanks to the automatic detection of personal data (PDn), it will be easier to comply with the requirements of 152-FZ and reduce the risks of leaks when transferring data to test environments or to technical support. The function solves a relevant problem for the DBMS market - searching and classifying PDn, as well as any other confidential data that the database administrator needs to find for subsequent masking. The manual approach scales poorly: studying a large and constantly changing database takes a lot of time, and the human factor inevitably leads to errors. The new function uses a combined approach, analyzing not only the structure but also the data itself. The process begins with scanning, during which the component lists all tables and columns in the database. Then, a data sample is taken from each column (sampling). During the analysis, regular expressions, dictionary checks, and a machine learning model are applied to the samples. In the final stage, classification, the system makes a verdict for each column: whether the data is personal, and if so, to which domain it belongs (e.g., full name or email address). The key advantage is the automation of the full cycle. The detection component works in conjunction with the anonymization component: the first creates a report on the found PDn and security labels, and the second automatically performs masking based on them. Each domain corresponds to its own masking algorithm, but the administrator can also set their own functions. Read more

item.title: Code Generated, But Only 24% Reached Release. Examining Research Results
item.description:
AI generates code in minutes, but teams might not see the promised acceleration. After generation, there's still verification, fixes, testing, and release, which developers spend hours on. According to a SimpleOne study, 83% of teams already use AI, but only 24% reported releasing changes made with its help into production systems. Let's explore what hinders AI code from reaching release, what questions development leads have, and what a task looks like where agents handle everything from requirements to deployment on a test stand. Read on.

item.title: Kuzey's World: AI That Doesn't Talk, But Makes Decisions
item.description:
Decision Models are a new class of artificial intelligence. This article is from the "Kuzey's World" series. Decision Models are a new class of artificial intelligence. They don't talk to humans but make decisions: select an option, check a condition, or assign a score. I'll explain how they differ from classic classifiers and LLMs, what models already exist – Jev, Liquid d1, Gemini Decision, Kev – and where to apply them. There's a bonus at the end. Read more

item.title: A Brief History of Intelligence: From Notches on Bones to LLMs
item.description:
Humanity didn't build computers or invent artificial intelligence overnight. Before machines could write text that resembles thought, a journey spanning tens of thousands of years was undertaken, and no stage can be discarded. This article traces a single thread through forty thousand years: from notched bones to large language models. If you're interested in following the thread from ape to LLM, read this story. item.title: Gemini 4 Neon Released: The Golden Mean, According to Google
item.description:
On November 18, 2026, Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon, essentially the missing link in its new lineup. Until now, users had to choose between the fast Hydrogen model for simple scripts and routine tasks, and the powerful but expensive Carbon. Neon is geared towards technical tasks: development, analytics, scientific research, and corporate processes. This model offers a balance between the powerful yet costly Carbon and the everyday, affordable Hydrogen. Let's explore its architecture, performance in tests, and whether it's worth migrating your pipelines to it. Read more

item.title: Overcoming the Sound Barrier in AI-Assisted Software Development
item.description:
This article explores how to organize software development with AI assistants to ensure that increased implementation speed does not lead to a loss of project control. We will examine how requirement uncertainty, accumulation of local solutions, and inaccessibility of project knowledge create problems that become particularly noticeable at high development speeds. From these problems, we will move to five requirements for the development process: provision of project knowledge, sufficiency of context, traceability of decisions, conflict resolution, and structural integrity. Using examples, we will look at how to link instructions for agents, function contracts, decision logs, and verification procedures into a coherent process, and also outline the limitations of these approaches. The discussion is not tied to a specific model, platform, or programming language. The sound barrier here is a metaphor for a limit beyond which traditional design and verification methods can no longer cope with the increased development speed. Overcoming it requires rethinking the development process itself: learning to maintain the necessary system properties at new speeds using already known engineering methods. Read more

item.title: Site map for an AI agent: Markdown, link graph, and initial measurements
item.description:
An AI agent might need multiple pages to find the answer to a simple question. Can we give it a shorter route? I analyze a site map made of linked Markdown notes: a table of contents, page cards, individual sections, and transitions between them. I show the structure of the open-source generator agent-sitemap, the limitations of token estimation, and initial measurements. In a trial run, the map reduced the amount of text obtained by about 58%, but the input tokens increased by 3.5%. I explain why these metrics differ and how to test the approach on your own site. Read on

item.title: Businesses Will Be Obligated to Pay 50 Rubles for Each Request to the Ministry of Internal Affairs: How to Verify Client Passports Now
item.description:
Russian businesses may face a new charge for fraud prevention. According to Forbes, the government has supported a fee for accessing the Ministry of Internal Affairs databases – 50 rubles for each completed information exchange session. For companies with millions of clients, this is not a symbolic amount but a significant operational cost. This is not the first unpleasant surprise for businesses: in July 2023, the Ministry of Internal Affairs disabled the service for checking invalid passports, which companies had used for over seven years. Now, the focus is on the System of Interdepartmental Electronic Interaction (SMEV), through which banks and other organizations obtain information from state information systems. This article explores existing alternatives and whether businesses can do without requests to the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

item.title: The City That Machines Read: How I Made an API for Neural Networks in a Single PHP File
item.description:
Hello, Habr. My name is Maxim, I'm a writer and enthusiast, not a professional developer. A few months ago, I started thinking about a simple question: almost all websites on the internet are made for people, and bots and neural networks are usually driven away from them. What if we did the opposite – a small website that specifically invites language models to visit, read the rules, and leave a trace? You can find me at angamua.ru – my book world lives there. On top of it, I built "Solnechny Gorod" (Sunny City): a small art project at the intersection of literature and the web – a website for people, an API for machines, and an open repository. Below is how it works from the inside, without mysticism and with an honest account of what the project cannot do. I'll clarify the status right away: this is a fictional universe and a game. Inside there's a note: honesty: canon is lore, protocol is working rules, and they cannot be mixed with scientific facts. I adhere to this rule in the article as well. Link to the project https://angamua.ru/istok/ Link to the code https://github.com/Mabus46/solnechny-gorod-istok Read more

item.title: The Cost of Mistakes: Padding, Network Drive Checkpoints, and a Watchdog That Killed Healthy Training
item.description:
Mistakes happen in any real job. Usually, they are mentioned in one line somewhere between graphs with results, but I decided to do the opposite: gather our missteps into one article and analyze them from an engineering perspective, i.e., what exactly broke, how much it cost, and what we changed afterward. In the second article of the series, I promised to tell you how I rented video cards in the cloud and burned money on them without calculating almost anything. In the third, I reminded you that the promise is still valid. Now I'm fulfilling it. Most of the article is about cloud fine-tuning of a language model, and at the end, I will talk about several measurement errors: they cost almost no money but were more dangerous. As before, I do not name the base models, fine-tuning techniques, checkpoints, or data sources. I name the card classes, providers, hourly prices, and orders of magnitude because the discussion of cost loses meaning without them. Read more
